questions.scenario: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation across a shared repository. You are responsible for integrating it into the development workflow, including CLAUDE.md configuration, custom slash commands, and deciding when to use plan mode versus direct execution.
questions.stem: A senior engineer spent a week tuning Claude's behavior for the repository: naming conventions, the preferred error-handling pattern, and a reminder to use the internal logging wrapper. Claude follows these rules perfectly for her. A developer who joined on Monday cloned the same repository, but Claude ignores every one of the conventions in his sessions. She confirms she wrote the rules in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Send the new developer a copy of her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so he can paste it into his own home directory and keep the two copies in sync by hand.
Restate the conventions with stronger wording such as IMPORTANT and MUST so Claude gives them more weight in every developer's session.
Move the team conventions into the project's CLAUDE.md (repository root or .claude/CLAUDE.md) and commit it so everyone who clones the repo loads them.
Move the conventions into CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root so they sit next to the code and load automatically for anyone working there.

questions.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is **user-level** memory: it applies only to the person whose home directory it lives in and never travels through version control. Conventions the whole team needs belong in **project-level** memory (`./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`), which is committed and loaded for everyone who works in the repo. This is the classic hierarchy diagnosis: the instructions are at the wrong scope, not phrased badly.

whyWrong.A: Manual copying works for one person today but drifts as soon as either copy changes and must be repeated for every new hire. Version control already solves distribution.
whyWrong.B: Emphasis cannot help when the file is never loaded. The new developer's session doesn't contain these instructions at all.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.local.md is meant for personal, project-specific notes and should be gitignored, so teammates still would not get it.

questions.mindset: When behavior differs between people, check the scope of the instruction before its wording.

questions.scenario: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation across a shared repository. You are responsible for integrating it into the development workflow, including CLAUDE.md configuration, custom slash commands, and deciding when to use plan mode versus direct execution.
questions.stem: Your monorepo has twelve packages. The platform team maintains separate standards documents in docs/standards/ (security.md, react.md, graphql.md, data-retention.md, python-style.md). The maintainers of each package know exactly which of these apply to their code: the Python services never touch React, and only two packages handle personal data. You want each package's CLAUDE.md to bring in the right standards while keeping a single source of truth for each document. What should you do?

options.text: In each package's CLAUDE.md, add @ imports (such as @../../docs/standards/security.md) for only the standards its maintainers say apply.
Paste all five standards documents into the root CLAUDE.md so every package automatically receives every standard regardless of its tech stack.
Copy the relevant sections of each standards document into the individual package CLAUDE.md files so each package is fully self-contained.
Convert each standards document into a skill so Claude can decide on its own which standards to load whenever it works inside a package.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md supports `@path` imports, which pull another file's contents into memory. Relative paths resolve from the **importing file**, not from where Claude was launched. Letting each package's maintainers import only the relevant standards keeps memory **modular** and keeps each standard in **one place**, so an update to security.md reaches every package that imports it. One nuance: if a developer launches Claude from inside a package, `../../docs/...` resolves outside the working directory, so Claude Code shows a one-time approval dialog for those external imports; after approval they load normally.

whyWrong.B: This floods every session with standards that don't apply (React rules in Python services), wasting context and inviting misapplied guidance.
whyWrong.C: Copying creates many diverging copies of each standard. When the platform team updates a document, the package copies go stale.
whyWrong.D: Skills load on demand when invoked by a user or chosen by the model. Standards that must always apply in a package belong in always-loaded memory, not something Claude may or may not pick.

questions.mindset: Use @import to compose memory from a single source of truth, scoped by people who know what applies.

questions.scenario: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation across a shared repository. You are responsible for integrating it into the development workflow, including CLAUDE.md configuration, custom slash commands, and deciding when to use plan mode versus direct execution.
questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to about 700 lines covering testing, API conventions, deployment steps, and code style. Pull requests that touch it regularly hit merge conflicts, and reviewers struggle to find the section they own. Every one of these standards must still be in context for every session, regardless of which files Claude touches. Which TWO changes improve maintainability while meeting that requirement? Choose TWO.

options.text: Convert each section into a skill in .claude/skills/ so the content is only loaded when a developer invokes it or Claude decides it is relevant.
Split the sections into focused files such as .claude/rules/testing.md, api-conventions.md and deployment.md, with no paths frontmatter.
Split the sections into .claude/rules/ files and add paths frontmatter to each one so it only loads for the directories it describes.
Move each section into the personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md of the engineers who own that area, so ownership is clear and conflicts disappear.
Move each section into its own file under docs/claude/ and reference those files from a short root CLAUDE.md with @ imports.

questions.explanation: Both correct options break a monolith into owned, focused files **without changing what loads**. Rule files in `.claude/rules/` that have **no `paths` frontmatter** load at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. `@` imports are also resolved at launch. Either way, every standard is still present in every session, but each topic now lives in its own file, so owners edit separately and conflicts drop.

whyWrong.A: Skills are on-demand. The stem's buried qualifier says every standard must always be in context, and skills don't guarantee that.
whyWrong.C: Adding `paths` makes a rule conditional: it loads only when Claude reads a matching file. That breaks the requirement that the standards apply regardless of which files Claude touches.
whyWrong.D: User-level memory isn't shared through version control, so the rules would disappear for everyone except the owner of each file.

questions.mindset: Modularize for maintainability, but check whether the mechanism changes when content loads.

questions.stem: Two developers on the same project report that Claude behaves differently for them: for one it always uses the team's test fixtures, for the other it ignores them. Both say they are on the latest commit and launch Claude from the repository root. Before changing any instructions, what is the MOST useful first diagnostic step?

options.text: Switch both developers to the largest available model so instruction-following becomes more consistent across their sessions.
Have each developer run /context in their session and compare the Memory files lists to see which CLAUDE.md and rules files actually loaded.
Rewrite the fixture instruction in capital letters and move it to the very top of the project CLAUDE.md so it can't be overlooked.
Ask Claude at the end of each session to confirm in writing that it followed the fixture instruction, and log the answers.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent behavior across people is usually a **loading** problem: a personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` that adds or contradicts guidance, a `claudeMdExcludes` setting, or a file that simply isn't in context for one of them. The documented first step when Claude isn't following CLAUDE.md is to run `/context` and check the list under **Memory files**, which shows exactly which CLAUDE.md and rules files loaded in the current session. Comparing the two lists exposes the difference directly. Diagnose what was loaded before you tune wording or models. (Note: `/memory` lists memory file *locations*, including files that don't exist yet, and opens them for editing; `/context` is the command that shows what is actually in the session.)

whyWrong.A: A bigger model doesn't fix an instruction that isn't in context, or one contradicted by another loaded file. It's an expensive guess made before the cause is known.
whyWrong.C: This changes wording before the cause is known. If one developer's session never loads that file, or a personal file contradicts it, emphasis changes nothing.
whyWrong.D: Model self-reports are not a diagnostic. They don't show which files loaded and can be wrong.

questions.mindset: Verify what is loaded before you change what is written.

questions.stem: A team is restructuring its Claude Code memory with @ imports. During review, engineers make several claims about how imports behave. Which TWO claims are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: A relative path in an @ import is resolved relative to the file that contains the import, not relative to the directory Claude was launched from.
Imported files are loaded lazily, only when Claude reads a source file that mentions the imported file's name, so imports reduce context usage.
Instructions in an imported file override conflicting instructions in the importing CLAUDE.md, giving imports the highest priority.
Imported files are loaded when the session starts, so splitting content into imports organizes memory but doesn't make it cheaper in context.
An @ import written inside a fenced code block is still evaluated, which makes code blocks a convenient way to group several imports.

questions.explanation: Per the memory docs, relative import paths resolve **relative to the importing file**, and imported files are expanded and loaded **at launch** together with the CLAUDE.md that references them. Imports therefore help with organization and reuse, not with context cost. For conditional loading, use path-scoped rules in `.claude/rules/` or on-demand skills.

whyWrong.B: Imports aren't lazy. They load with the importing file. Path-scoped rules and skills are the on-demand mechanisms.
whyWrong.C: Memory content is combined, not ranked by an override system that favors imports. Imported text simply becomes part of the importing file's context.
whyWrong.E: Imports inside code spans and fenced code blocks are deliberately **not** evaluated, so you can show `@` syntax in examples without triggering an import.

questions.mindset: Know which mechanisms organize context and which ones actually defer it.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling with Claude. Engineers use it to explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and a few MCP servers.
questions.stem: One engineer wants Claude to use her personal sandbox database URL and give extra-detailed explanations, but only when she works in this one legacy repository. These preferences must not reach teammates, and she doesn't want them in the other projects she works on. Where should she put them?

options.text: In the project's root CLAUDE.md, under a heading that says the section applies only to her, so Claude can tell when to use it.
In her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, because user-level memory is personal and is never shared with teammates through version control.
In a CLAUDE.md inside a subdirectory she created for her own scratch work, so the file only loads when Claude reads files there.
In a CLAUDE.local.md at the root of this repository, with the file excluded from version control through .gitignore.

questions.explanation: `CLAUDE.local.md` is the **local** scope: personal, project-specific instructions that load alongside the project CLAUDE.md for this repository only and are kept out of git. It meets both qualifiers in the stem: hidden from teammates **and** limited to this one project.

whyWrong.A: The committed project file loads for everyone. A heading asking Claude to apply a section to only one person relies on inference and also exposes her sandbox URL to the team.
whyWrong.B: User-level memory is private, but it applies across **all** her projects, which breaks the 'only this repository' requirement.
whyWrong.C: A subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads only when Claude reads files in that subdirectory, so her preferences would be missing most of the time, and the file could be committed by accident.

questions.mindset: Match the memory scope to exactly two questions: who should see it, and where it should apply.

questions.scenario: Your organization runs Claude Code inside its CI/CD pipeline to perform automated code reviews, generate test cases and leave feedback on pull requests. The pipeline must produce actionable feedback with few false positives.
questions.stem: The repository's CLAUDE.md says: 'Never modify files under db/migrations/; propose changes in the PR comment instead.' In the CI pipeline, Claude follows this most of the time, but twice this month an automated run edited a migration file, which caused a failed deploy. Leadership wants this to never happen again, with the least ongoing maintenance. What should the team do?

options.text: Move the rule to the first line of CLAUDE.md, mark it CRITICAL, and add three examples of correct behavior so the instruction is harder to miss.
Add a permission deny rule such as Edit(db/migrations/**) to the project settings the CI job uses, and keep the CLAUDE.md note as explanatory context.
Add a final step to the CI prompt asking Claude to review its own diff and revert any changes it made to migration files before finishing.
Run a second Claude instance after each job that reads the diff and comments on the PR whenever a migration file was modified.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is delivered as **context**, not enforcement, so Claude follows it most of the time, not every time. When the requirement is 'never', use a **deterministic control**. Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code itself, not by the model, and deny rules apply in **every** permission mode, including `bypassPermissions`, which CI jobs often use. A path-scoped `Edit(...)` deny rule blocks the built-in editing tools and also the file-writing shell commands and redirects Claude Code recognizes, so the edit is stopped before it happens, with nothing to maintain afterward. (A `PreToolUse` hook that blocks writes to that folder is the other deterministic option.) CLAUDE.md can still explain *why* the rule exists.

whyWrong.A: Stronger wording and examples raise compliance but still rely on the model reading and honoring the instruction on every run. It remains probabilistic.
whyWrong.C: Self-review is another probabilistic step done by the same model that made the mistake, and by then the edit has already happened.
whyWrong.D: This detects the problem after the fact instead of preventing it, adds a second model call to every run, and still lets the bad edit land in the PR.

questions.mindset: CLAUDE.md informs; permissions and hooks enforce. 'Never' calls for an enforcement mechanism.

questions.stem: A developer launches Claude Code from the root of a monorepo. The repository has a root CLAUDE.md and also packages/billing/CLAUDE.md, which holds currency-rounding conventions. Early in the session, the developer asks a general design question about billing, and Claude's answer ignores the rounding conventions. Later, after Claude has opened several files in packages/billing/, its answers follow them. What BEST explains this?

options.text: The root CLAUDE.md overrides any nested CLAUDE.md until the developer explicitly reloads memory, at which point the nested file takes precedence.
Nested CLAUDE.md files are only honored when the root CLAUDE.md references them with an @ import, which explains why the conventions applied inconsistently.
Nested CLAUDE.md files are only read when they are committed to version control and Claude has refreshed its view of the git status.
CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories below the launch directory load on demand when Claude reads files in that subtree, not at session start.

questions.explanation: At launch Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files from the working directory **and its ancestors**. CLAUDE.md files in **descendant** directories are loaded **on demand** when Claude reads files in those directories. Before Claude touched packages/billing/, the billing conventions weren't in context. Once it read files there, they were. To have them from the start, launch from that package or ask Claude to read a file there first.

whyWrong.A: Memory files are **combined**, not overridden. More specific files add to broader ones, and no manual reload is involved in this behavior.
whyWrong.B: Nested CLAUDE.md files load on their own when files in their directory are read. No import from the root is needed.
whyWrong.C: Loading depends on file location and what Claude reads, not on git status or whether the file is committed.

questions.mindset: Know when each memory file enters context: ancestors at launch, descendants on demand.

questions.scenario: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation across a shared repository. You are responsible for integrating it into the development workflow, including CLAUDE.md configuration, custom slash commands, and deciding when to use plan mode versus direct execution.
questions.stem: A production alert includes a full stack trace pointing to a null dereference on line 88 of invoice_formatter.py. The function is short, the cause is visible in the trace (an optional discount field is not checked), and the team already agreed on the fix: return the undiscounted total when the field is missing. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use direct execution: give Claude the stack trace and the agreed fix, let it edit the function, and have it add a regression test.
Enter plan mode so Claude can survey the whole billing package and propose several candidate designs before touching the file.
Launch an Explore subagent to map every caller of the formatter across the repository before deciding whether a change is needed.
Write a detailed design document for the fix first, then start a fresh session and give Claude the document as context.

questions.explanation: Direct execution fits **well-scoped, well-understood** changes: one file, a clear stack trace, and an agreed fix. The official guidance is that plan mode adds overhead and is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, the change spans multiple files, or the code is unfamiliar; if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. None of the plan-mode signals apply here, so planning would only add cost.

whyWrong.B: No design choice is open. The fix is already decided, so exploring alternatives costs time without reducing risk.
whyWrong.C: Wide discovery is for verbose, open-ended investigation. The trace already pins the problem to one function.
whyWrong.D: A design document for a one-line guard clause is process overhead with no benefit.

questions.mindset: Match process to uncertainty: when scope and fix are both clear, execute directly.

questions.scenario: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation across a shared repository. You are responsible for integrating it into the development workflow, including CLAUDE.md configuration, custom slash commands, and deciding when to use plan mode versus direct execution.
questions.stem: The team must replace a deprecated HTTP client library with a newer one. A quick search shows about 50 call sites across services, some using retry hooks and custom interceptors the new library handles differently. Engineers disagree on whether to wrap the new client behind an internal adapter or call it directly everywhere. The tech lead wants to avoid half-finished rework. What is the BEST way to start?

options.text: Use direct execution file by file, starting with the simplest call sites, and switch to plan mode only if Claude runs into an interceptor it can't migrate.
Write a very detailed prompt that specifies the exact replacement for every call pattern, then run the whole migration with direct execution.
Start in plan mode so Claude can explore the call sites, surface how interceptors and retries are used, and propose an approach to approve before any edits.
Open one Claude session per service and run them in parallel with direct execution so the migration finishes before the patterns diverge.

questions.explanation: This task has every signal that calls for plan mode: **many files**, **several valid approaches** (adapter versus direct calls), and behavior differences that are not fully understood yet. In plan mode Claude explores read-only and produces a plan for you to review **before** changing anything, so the adapter decision is made once, deliberately, instead of being discovered halfway through 50 edits.

whyWrong.A: The complexity is already known from the stem. Waiting until problems appear is exactly how half-finished rework happens.
whyWrong.B: Upfront instructions can't anticipate the interceptor and retry cases nobody has examined yet. Exploration has to come first.
whyWrong.D: Parallel sessions without an agreed approach produce inconsistent migrations across services. The open design question is the bottleneck, not speed.

questions.mindset: If the design choice is still open and the change is wide, plan before you edit.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling with Claude. Engineers use it to explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and a few MCP servers.
questions.stem: An engineer uses Claude to understand a 15-year-old order-processing system before adding a feature. The discovery phase involves dozens of Grep and Read calls that return long outputs. In previous attempts, by the time discovery finished, the main conversation was so full that Claude lost track of earlier decisions during implementation. What is the MOST effective change?

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window so that discovery output and implementation both fit in a single conversation.
Run /clear as soon as discovery ends, then start implementation in an empty conversation so nothing crowds out the new work.
Have Claude paste the raw discovery output into CLAUDE.md so the findings reload automatically at the start of every later session.
Delegate discovery to the Explore subagent, which keeps the verbose search output in its own context and returns only a summary.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent is built for verbose discovery. It runs read-only in its **own context window** and returns a **summary**. The main conversation keeps the conclusions but not the noise, so it has room for implementation and earlier decisions are not crowded out.

whyWrong.A: A bigger window postpones the problem. The context is still filled with low-value raw output, and attention to earlier decisions still degrades.
whyWrong.B: /clear discards everything, including the findings that discovery was meant to produce.
whyWrong.C: Raw search output in CLAUDE.md adds noise to every future session. Memory is for durable conventions, not transient tool output.

questions.mindset: Isolate noisy exploration and pass only the distilled result back.

questions.stem: A team lead is writing guidance on when to start Claude Code in plan mode. Which TWO of these tasks most clearly benefit from plan mode rather than direct execution? Choose TWO.

options.text: Adding a conditional that rejects end dates earlier than start dates in one existing validation function, plus a unit test for it.
Correcting a misspelled word in a user-facing error message that appears in a single template file used on the checkout page.
Choosing between a message queue and synchronous webhooks for a new integration, where each option needs different infrastructure.
Renaming a local variable inside one function so that it matches the naming convention documented in the team's style guide.
Splitting a shared authentication module out of a monolith into a standalone service used by several applications.

questions.explanation: Plan mode is designed for tasks with **architectural implications**, **several valid approaches** or **wide multi-file impact**. Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure (C) and extracting a shared module into a service (E) both need exploration and a reviewed design before edits. The other tasks are small and clearly scoped, which suits direct execution.

whyWrong.A: This is one conditional in one function with clear intent: a textbook direct-execution change.
whyWrong.B: A one-word fix in a single file has no design choice to plan.
whyWrong.D: A local rename inside one function is mechanical and contained.

questions.mindset: Plan mode is for uncertainty and blast radius, not for every change.

questions.scenario: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation across a shared repository. You are responsible for integrating it into the development workflow, including CLAUDE.md configuration, custom slash commands, and deciding when to use plan mode versus direct execution.
questions.stem: Your team is adopting a standard workflow for large changes such as moving the codebase to a new ORM. Leadership wants to avoid rework from a wrong approach, but also doesn't want to slow down the routine edits once the approach is settled. Which workflow BEST meets both goals?

options.text: Stay in plan mode for the entire migration, re-planning before each file is edited, so every individual change gets a reviewed design.
Use plan mode to explore and produce a migration plan that the team reviews and approves, then implement the approved plan with direct execution.
Use direct execution throughout and rely on checkpoints to rewind whenever an approach turns out to be wrong partway through.
Have engineers write the migration plan by hand outside Claude Code, then give it to Claude in direct execution so no tokens are spent on exploration.

questions.explanation: The recommended pattern **combines** the two modes: plan mode for investigation and design, which prevents costly rework, then direct execution for implementation once the approach is approved. Each mode handles the part it suits, which meets both of leadership's goals.

whyWrong.A: Re-planning routine per-file edits adds overhead after the design is settled, which conflicts with the 'don't slow down' goal.
whyWrong.C: Rewinding is recovery after wasted work, not prevention. Checkpoints also don't capture files changed through Bash commands, and they are not a substitute for version control.
whyWrong.D: A hand-written plan skips Claude's codebase exploration, which is what surfaces dependencies people miss. It optimizes tokens at the expense of quality.

questions.mindset: Plan first to decide, then execute directly to deliver.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling with Claude. Engineers use it to explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and a few MCP servers.
questions.stem: Engineers must add multi-tenant support to an internal analytics platform. The change will touch the database schema, the API layer, the caching layer and background jobs, and nobody on the current team wrote the original caching code. A senior engineer argues: 'Plan mode is slow. I'll write a thorough prompt describing exactly what to change, and Claude can execute it directly.' Which response BEST reflects sound Claude Code practice?

options.text: Use plan mode first, because exploring the unfamiliar caching and job code will surface dependencies that a prompt written upfront can't anticipate.
Agree, because a sufficiently detailed prompt removes the need for exploration, and direct execution finishes faster on large changes.
Agree, but add an instruction telling Claude to stop and ask whenever it is unsure, which gives the same safety as plan mode.
Use direct execution on the database schema first, then decide whether plan mode is needed based on how many files that change breaks.

questions.explanation: The stem names the signals for plan mode: **cross-cutting, architectural change** across several layers, plus **unknown code** nobody on the team understands. A detailed prompt can only describe what the author already knows. Plan mode lets Claude explore the real code read-only and propose a design you can correct **before** edits, which avoids the rework that hidden dependencies would cause.

whyWrong.B: Detail can't replace knowledge the author doesn't have. The unfamiliar caching layer is exactly where the prompt will be wrong.
whyWrong.C: 'Ask when unsure' relies on Claude noticing its own uncertainty while editing. It's weaker than reviewing a complete plan before any change.
whyWrong.D: Changing the schema first and measuring the breakage is discovery through damage. It creates the rework that planning prevents.

questions.mindset: A detailed prompt captures what you know; plan mode discovers what you don't.

questions.stem: In plan mode, Claude has explored the codebase and presented a plan for adding rate limiting. Reading it, the developer notices the plan stores counters in process memory, but the service runs as several replicas behind a load balancer, so counters must be shared. The developer hasn't approved anything yet. What should the developer do?

options.text: Approve the plan and fix the storage choice during implementation, since editing code directly is faster than revising a document.
Exit plan mode and implement the shared counter storage by hand, then ask Claude to finish the rest of the plan afterward.
Stay in plan mode, tell Claude about the multi-replica constraint, and have it revise the plan before approving any edits.
Discard the session and start a new one with a longer prompt that lists every infrastructure constraint the service has.

questions.explanation: The point of plan mode is to catch design mistakes **before** they become code. The plan approval prompt includes a **'No, keep planning'** choice precisely so you can stay in plan mode and tell Claude what to change; you can also open the plan in your editor to adjust it directly. A flaw found during review costs a sentence of feedback, while the same flaw found after implementation costs rework. Give the missing constraint and let Claude revise. The exploration context already gathered stays in the session.

whyWrong.A: Approving a plan you know is wrong turns a cheap fix into implementation rework and may spread the flawed design across files.
whyWrong.B: Splitting the work by hand risks inconsistency with the rest of the plan and gives up the help plan mode offers at exactly this step.
whyWrong.D: Restarting throws away the exploration already done. Feedback on the current plan is cheaper and keeps that context.

questions.mindset: Fix design flaws in the plan, where they are cheapest to fix.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling with Claude. Engineers use it to explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and a few MCP servers.
questions.stem: An engineer wants Claude to remove a deprecated internal API from a large monorepo. The work has three phases: find every call site and how it is used (the searches return very long output), decide on a replacement strategy for three distinct usage patterns, then make the edits. An earlier attempt failed because the context filled up during phase one, and Claude then chose inconsistent replacements. Which TWO changes are MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Switch to the model with the largest context window so the whole three-phase task fits in one conversation without other changes.
Delegate phase one to the Explore subagent so the long search output stays in its context and only a summary of call sites and patterns returns.
Disable CLAUDE.md for this session to free up context for the search results during the discovery phase.
Use plan mode for phase two so Claude proposes one replacement strategy per usage pattern for review before any edits begin.
Run everything with direct execution and use /compact after every few files so the context never fills up.

questions.explanation: The two failures have two different fixes. **Context exhaustion** during verbose discovery is solved by isolating that phase in the **Explore subagent**, which returns a summary. **Inconsistent replacements** come from deciding the strategy ad hoc, which is solved by producing and approving a **plan** before editing. Together they follow the documented pattern of isolated discovery, then a planned design, then execution.

whyWrong.A: A bigger window delays exhaustion but does nothing about inconsistent strategy, and still fills the context with raw search output.
whyWrong.C: CLAUDE.md holds the conventions the edits should follow. Removing it saves little and makes the result worse.
whyWrong.E: Repeated compaction summarizes away detail as work goes on, and with no agreed strategy the replacements can still be inconsistent.

questions.mindset: Diagnose each failure separately: isolate noisy discovery, and plan before acting on open design choices.
